---
title: Build an agent app
description: How Nyte's packages fit together, and how to build your own terminal, web, or editor app on them
---

Nyte's TUI and desktop app are built from the same packages you can use. This page walks through
how those pieces fit, why we split them where we did, and how to put them back together in a
different shape.

The packages are private workspace packages that export TypeScript source, so you'll work from a
checkout of the repository.

## How it's put together

```text
@nyte-ai/ai                 models, providers, credentials
        |
@nyte-ai/host               model + storage + plugin composition
        |
@nyte-ai/core               sessions, messages, agent execution
        |\
        | local SDK -> your terminal interface
        |
@nyte-ai/server             JSON calls + SSE watches
        |
@nyte-ai/client             transport, observer, outbox, projections
        |
your interface

@nyte-ai/app                React conversation + workbench
        |
NyteBridge                 desktop IPC or web client
```

Read it from the top. `@nyte-ai/core` is the part that matters most. It stores every session the
way git stores a repository, as immutable objects plus a few refs that move, and it runs the agent
against that history. `@nyte-ai/host` makes the choices a real app has to make on top of core:
which models answer, which plugins load, and whether a folder is trusted.

Everything below core is about reaching it. You get the same SDK whether you hold it in your own
process or talk to it over HTTP, so an interface written against one works against the other. We
did this because the TUI, the desktop app, and the web app all needed the same conversation, and
we didn't want three ways of reading it.

## Sending a message doesn't run it

This is the one idea to have in your head before writing code. `messages.send` writes the message
to the session's inbox and returns. It doesn't call a model. A process that has called
`attach()` picks the message up and runs it. If no process has attached, `runs.wait` waits
forever.

We split it this way so a session outlives the process that started it. The message is durable
the moment `send` returns. If the runner crashes halfway through, the work so far is already in the
store, and another runner can carry on once the first one's lease expires. Interfaces can come
and go while the agent keeps working, and several of them can watch the same session at once.

In practice your host calls `attach()` once at startup and keeps it until shutdown. Your interface
only sends and watches.

## Build your own host

`createHost` builds the SDK from a model catalog, a store, and a plugin policy. Start with chat
mode, which has no project folder and no filesystem tools:

```ts title="Conversation host"
import process from "node:process";
import { createNyteModels } from "@nyte-ai/ai";
import { SqliteStore } from "@nyte-ai/core/store";
import { createHost, resolveModel } from "@nyte-ai/host";

const models = createNyteModels();
const model = await resolveModel(models, process.env.NYTE_MODEL ?? "openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol");
const store = new SqliteStore("./agent.db");

try {
  const sdk = await createHost({
    models,
    model,
    store,
    plugins: { kind: "chat", system: "You are a helpful assistant." },
  });
  const detach = sdk.attach();

  try {
    const session = await sdk.sessions.create();
    await sdk.messages.send({
      sessionId: session.sessionId,
      content: "Hello",
      key: crypto.randomUUID(),
    });
    await sdk.runs.wait({ sessionId: session.sessionId });
    const snapshot = await sdk.sessions.snapshot({ sessionId: session.sessionId });
    process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(snapshot, null, 2)}\n`);
  } finally {
    detach();
    await sdk.close();
  }
} finally {
  await store.close();
}
```

The host reads credentials from Nyte's provider sign-in or from provider environment variables.
`key` makes the send idempotent. Send twice with the same key and you get one message, which is
what lets clients retry safely later on.

### Give it a workspace

A coding agent needs a folder to work in. Swap the plugin policy for workspace mode and pass a
workspace backend:

```ts title="Workspace host"
import process from "node:process";
import { createHost, createWorkspaceBackend, createWorkspaceStore } from "@nyte-ai/host";

const workspaces = createWorkspaceStore();
const workspace = await workspaces.require(process.cwd());

const sdk = await createHost({
  models,
  model,
  store,
  workspace: createWorkspaceBackend(workspaces),
  plugins: {
    kind: "workspace",
    target: { kind: "project", workspace },
  },
});
```

`require()` throws unless the user has already trusted the folder. Ask them first, then call
`workspaces.trust(cwd)`. Be honest with them about what that means. Trust lets project plugins run
and gives the agent unrestricted tools in that folder. It isn't a sandbox, and Nyte doesn't ask
per tool call. We chose one clear decision per folder over a stream of prompts people learn to
click through.

Workspace mode loads the shared built-ins, your home and project plugins, and skills. To share
history with the TUI and desktop app, open the store at `workspaceStorePath(workspace.cwd)`
instead of `./agent.db`.

If you're embedding Nyte in your own product and want to choose every plugin yourself, use
`{ kind: "custom", plugins, cwd }`.

## Build your own TUI

Keep the host and write your own rendering. You need two things from `@nyte-ai/client`. The
`SessionObserver` keeps an up-to-date view of the session. The outbox holds the messages the user
has typed but the store hasn't confirmed yet.

```ts title="Conversation state"
import { createOutbox, SessionObserver } from "@nyte-ai/client";

const observer = new SessionObserver(sdk, {
  sessionId: session.sessionId,
});
const outbox = createOutbox({
  send: (input) => sdk.messages.send(input),
});

const unsubscribeObserver = observer.subscribe((update) => {
  outbox.observe(update);
  draw(update.state, outbox.rows());
});
const unsubscribeOutbox = outbox.subscribe(() => {
  const state = observer.state;
  if (state !== undefined) draw(state, outbox.rows());
});

await observer.start();
await outbox.submit({
  sessionId: session.sessionId,
  content: "Explain this repository",
  delivery: "next",
});
```

`draw` is yours. It gets the session state and the pending rows, and renders both.

They're separate pieces because they solve different problems. The SDK itself never retries. A
call that fails throws, and a watch that drops just ends. The observer handles reading: it takes a
snapshot, follows live events, and starts over from a fresh snapshot when the watch breaks. The
outbox handles writing: it shows the message the moment the user hits enter, retries with the same
key until the send lands, and drops its copy once the observer sees the real one.

`delivery: "next"` queues the message for when the agent is idle. `"steer"` delivers it at the next
response boundary while the agent is still working.

When the view goes away, call both unsubscribe functions and `observer.close()`. That stops your
interface, not the agent. If unsent messages should survive a restart, give the outbox a `storage`
and call `activate()` on startup.

The shipped TUI wires these the same way in
[`packages/tui/src/interactive.ts`](https://github.com/interfaces-lab/nyte/blob/main/packages/tui/src/interactive.ts).

## Put the host behind a server

When the interface runs somewhere else, like a browser or another machine, put `@nyte-ai/server`
in front of the SDK:

```ts title="HTTP handler"
import { createNyteServer } from "@nyte-ai/server";

const server = createNyteServer({
  sdk,
  version: "1.0.0",
  auth: { kind: "token", token },
});

const handler = server.fetch;
```

The server is a plain `Request` to `Response` handler. Hand it to `Bun.serve`, `Deno.serve`, or a
Node adapter. It doesn't open a socket or attach a runner, because that's your process and your
decision. Tokens need at least 16 characters. Bind to loopback unless you've set up remote access
properly.

On shutdown, close in reverse order. Close the server and listener, detach the runner, close the
SDK, then close the store.

On the other side, create a client where you would have opened an SDK:

```ts title="Remote client"
import { createNyteClient } from "@nyte-ai/client";

const sdk = createNyteClient({
  baseUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:5180",
  token,
});
const session = await sdk.sessions.create();
```

Everything from the TUI section works unchanged with this `sdk`. That's the payoff of keeping one
SDK shape on both sides of the wire.

## Build your own editor

The desktop and web apps share one React app, `@nyte-ai/app`, which contains the conversation and
the workbench. The app never imports core. It reads everything through a `NyteBridge` on
`window.nyte`, which is the SDK plus host services like the terminal and the native browser.

That bridge is the seam. Desktop backs it with Electron IPC to a host running in the main
process. The web entry backs it with `createNyteClient`. Same app, two hosts. We drew the line
there so the renderer can't reach the filesystem or credentials directly, and so the app runs in a
browser without changes.

To build your own editor, give the app a bridge and mount it:

```tsx title="Mount the app"
import { App } from "@nyte-ai/app";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

createRoot(container).render(<App appIcon={appIcon} />);
```

The bridge has to be installed before any module that reads it loads. Copy the order from
[`packages/desktop/src/renderer/src/main.tsx`](https://github.com/interfaces-lab/nyte/blob/main/packages/desktop/src/renderer/src/main.tsx)
or the web entry at
[`packages/app/src/web/entry.tsx`](https://github.com/interfaces-lab/nyte/blob/main/packages/app/src/web/entry.tsx).
Both also handle fonts, styles, and router startup.

The workbench lives in `packages/app/src/workbench`:

| Module                | Implementation                                                      |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `workbench.tsx`       | Panel layout and dispatch for files, changes, browser, and terminal |
| `files-panel.tsx`     | File tree using `@pierre/trees`                                     |
| `file-editor.tsx`     | Editing using `@pierre/diffs`                                       |
| `terminal-runtime.ts` | Terminal rendering using `ghostty-web`                              |

Reuse the whole app rather than single panels. The panels depend on the app's stores, queries,
router, theme, and workers. The build setup for StyleX, source resolution, and WASM is in the app's
own config. Desktop gets interactive terminals from `@lydell/node-pty`. An HTTP client has no
terminal unless you provide a backend for one.

## Or extend what's already there

If you mostly like the TUI and want to change part of it, write a plugin instead. The TUI's
rendering, transcript, and composer are internal. Through `@nyte-ai/plugin` you can add tools to
sessions, listen to session events, show toasts, and render into the `session.composer.top` slot.
That's far less code to own.

## What there is to copy

| Path                              | What runs                                                          |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `packages/demo/server/cloudflare` | Local SQLite-backed Durable Object with alarm-driven execution     |
| `packages/demo/server/vercel`     | PostgreSQL-backed chat host with durable Vercel Workflow execution |
| `packages/demo/website`           | Static interface previews, not a live agent                        |

The server demos are chat only, with no workspace or terminal. They're worth reading for one
thing. Each shows a runner that isn't a long-lived process, which is the inbox design from the top
of this page doing its job. Setup lives in the
[Cloudflare guide](https://github.com/interfaces-lab/nyte/blob/main/packages/demo/server/cloudflare/README.md)
and the [Vercel guide](https://github.com/interfaces-lab/nyte/blob/main/packages/demo/server/vercel/README.md).

For a full app, the TUI and desktop are the examples. There's no separate starter for either.
